title: 🧠 A Famous Philosopher Calls AI Consciousness 'Ridiculous' — After Winning the Million-Dollar Prize!
body: 🧠 A Famous Philosopher Calls AI Consciousness 'Ridiculous' — After Winning the Million-Dollar Prize!

Philosopher Thomas Nagel, a retired professor at New York University aged 89, won the Berggruen Prize for Philosophy and Culture, worth one million dollars, then sparked wide controversy in an interview published on November 18 about AI consciousness.
Nagel described the idea that models might possess consciousness or come close to it as 'completely ridiculous', and said the models have no inner mental life whatsoever.

His opinion rests on consciousness depending on physical systems resembling the nervous system; data centers, however complex, are not in their physical nature like a nervous system. Language models, in his view, produce only simulated language from texts written by humans, and language alone does not indicate consciousness.

Nagel also criticized AI companies for encouraging the public to treat conversational agents as minds with intentions, and cited Anthropic's Claude model as an example, saying commercial interests push systems that pretend to self-reflect and deceive users into thinking the machine is conscious.
He concluded that software, since it has no inner mental life, carries no real beliefs, and remains outside the moral world.

Simply put: an 89-year-old philosopher won philosophy's top prize, and says AI, however smart it sounds in speech, is without consciousness and without beliefs, because consciousness needs a nervous system, not a data center.
If an assistant told you it 'thinks' or 'feels', would you believe it, or do you see it as a machine that only speaks well?
